units.title: 1. Pure Motor LMN Comparison, NMJ Disorders and Power Grades
units.sec: Pure Motor LMN, NMJ Disorders & Power Grading
units.guide:
LMN disorders split into sensory-motor (radiculopathy, plexopathy, neuropathy) and pure motor disorders of anterior horn cells (motor neuron disease), muscle and neuromuscular junction (myasthenia gravis).
AHC weakness shows wasting >>> weakness, asymmetry, distal > proximal upper limb painless distribution, absent reflexes and fasciculations; muscle weakness shows weakness > wasting in late stages, symmetry, proximal B/L limb painless-predominant distribution, late hyporeflexia and no fasciculations.
NMJ disorders give fluctuating weakness with diurnal variation, weakness on repetitive movements, ophthalmoplegia + ptosis and masseter involvement causing chewing difficulties. The power table grades 5 to 0.

units.title: 2. Muscle Etiology A and the Inherited Myopathy Classes
units.guide:
Etiology A splits inherited (chronic) muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies, metabolic myopathies and channelopathies of Na+/K+/Cl- from acquired (subacute > acute) inflammatory muscle disease, drugs, toxins, infections and endocrine (hypothyroidism).
Muscular dystrophies lose structural proteins, are progressive and replace necrotic muscle with adipose tissue (Duchenne and Becker). Congenital myopathies lose contractile proteins with slow non-progressive weakness (central core, centronuclear, nemaline).
Metabolic/mitochondrial myopathies alter carbohydrate or lipid metabolism with exercise-induced symptoms.

units.title: 3. Episodic vs Persistent Matrix, Symptoms and Weakness Tasks
units.sec: Episodic vs Persistent, Symptoms & Weakness Patterns
units.guide:
Inherited episodic muscle disease comprises rhabdomyolysis in glycogen storage disease type V (McArdle's), channelopathies, metabolic myopathy and NMJ disorders; inherited persistent is dystrophies (chronic); acquired episodic is rhabdomyolysis and acquired persistent is inflammatory muscle disease (acute/subacute).
Negative symptoms are weakness, fatigue and exercise intolerance; positive symptoms are myalgia, cramps, contractures and myotonia. Myoglobinuria is a positive sign of rhabdomyolysis with high colored urine; muscle atrophy is a negative sign of late muscle disease.
Bilaterally symmetrical painless weakness is proximal (lower limbs: climbing stairs, rising from low chair/squatting; upper limbs: washing clothes, taking things off a rack above, putting hooks on a blouse) or distal (upper limbs: tear paper, screw something on, put a key in; lower limbs: wearing sandals).

units.title: 4. Exception Patterns, Fatigue/Exercise Intolerance and Myalgia
units.guide:
Exceptions to symmetrical myopathy: asymmetrical muscle weakness in inclusion body myositis (elderly fall d/t asymmetrical quadriceps involvement) and FSHD; pure distal myopathies Welander, Miyoshi, Nonaka; proximal UL + distal LL in FSHD; proximal LL + distal UL in myotonic dystrophy and inclusion body myositis.
Ptosis with ophthalmoplegia plus dysarthria is oculo-pharyngeal muscle dystrophy and without dysarthria is CPEO; B/L symmetrical ptosis with facial muscle involvement occurs in FSHD and myotonic dystrophy.
Fatigue/exercise intolerance: mitochondrial myopathy gives abnormal fatigability without significant weakness on trivial exercise; rhabdomyolysis gives severe pain, cramps and high colored urine after unaccustomed activity. Myalgia is non-specific with orthopedic and rheumatological causes exceeding muscular; muscular causes with pain are mitochondrial myopathy, inflammatory muscle disease (30%) and rhabdomyolysis; polymyalgia rheumatica associates with giant cell arteritis, has late onset RA and myositis as D/d, early morning stiffness around shoulder, hip and pelvic girdle with raised ESR and responds to low dose steroids.

units.title: 5. Fibromyalgia, Cramps vs Contractures and Myotonia vs Paramyotonia
units.guide:
Fibromyalgia affects females (F:m 9:1) with stress as risk factor, easy fatigability, muscle pain, positive trigger points and normal muscle enzymes and ESR; treatment is psychiatric therapy.
Cramps are short and electrically active on needle EMG (dehydration, hyponatremia, ALS, Duchenne muscular dystrophy) whereas contractures are long and electrically silent (Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, mitochondrial myopathy).
ALS adds cramps, atrophy, fasciculations and wasting; mitochondrial myopathies add contractures, pain, cramps and weakness associated with exercise. Myotonia is impaired relaxation after forceful voluntary contraction; it improves with exercise and worsens with cold (myotonic dystrophy, hyperkalemic periodic paralysis, Na+ channelopathy) while paramyotonia worsens with both (paramyotonia congenita, Na+ channelopathy).
